name: Emeka Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say is confidential and won't be traced back to you. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the sales order desk at Calder Building Products. We make bricks, blocks and roof tiles, and my ten people take the orders from builders' merchants, check stock and get the lorries booked. I'm on the phone half the day myself, because the big customers want to talk to the manager when a delivery's late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the customers, honestly. Some of the yard managers I've dealt with for five years, and we ask after each other's families. What wears me out is head office sending new systems every year that nobody asked for. I'm 27, engaged to Grace, she teaches at the primary school, the wedding's next September, and we've got a flat my dad helped us buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Every year someone at head office says a new system will change everything, and every year my team still ends up phoning the customer to check what they meant. If AI goes the same way, I'm not surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads on the desk I told you so. At church or with friends I'd probably say the computer people oversold it again. I don't go online about work, never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I've never used one of these AI chat things and I'd rather not start. If it stays a gadget for emails, my job stays a job about people and phones, which is what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal, really. Keep the team as it is, keep putting money aside for the wedding and for a bigger place when children come. And go for the regional sales manager job when it opens next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Comfortable. A bit smug, maybe, which isn't a nice thing to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not start using AI. What puts you off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust a machine to know that when Mr Haldane at the Birchfield yard says the usual, he means 40 pallets of grey blocks and not 30. That kind of thing lives in people's heads. And I don't like typing our customers' business into something run by a tech company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about work that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Building's been slow this year, so orders are down about ten percent, and Calder's cut overtime in the factory. My desk's fine for now. But I'd be lying if I said it wasn't in my head.

say: I'd tell the lads on the desk **I told you so**.
The **computer people oversold it** again, I'd say at church.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because I've never used AI and don't want to.
My job stays about **people and phones**, which I'm good at.
do: **Carry on as normal** with the same ten-person team.
Keep saving for the **wedding** and a bigger place for children.
Apply for the **regional sales manager** job next year.
feel: **Comfortable**, maybe **a bit smug**, which isn't nice to admit.
S0.quote: Every year someone at head office says a new system will change everything, and every year my team still ends up phoning the customer to check what they meant.
fieldNote: He **distrusts AI** with customer knowledge that lives in people's heads.
A **ten percent drop** in orders and factory overtime cuts already sit on his mind.
He'd **never post** about work; his circle is the order desk and church.

steps.text: Keep the ten-person order desk running as it is
Apply for regional sales manager when it opens next year
Keep saving for the wedding and a bigger family home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one that bothers me. Booking, checking and answering customers is my order desk at the brick works, near enough word for word. Head office would love an excuse to send the orders straight into a computer and cut half my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be careful, because our customers like a person and they'll go to a competitor if they get a robot. With friends I'd say the big tech firms are selling bosses a dream to cut wages. I'd say it at church too, that work gives people dignity and you can't hand that to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd do it anyway, and I'd be on the wrong side of it. The managers who'll survive are the ones who can run the new system, and I've avoided all of that. I'd be one of maybe two desk managers fighting for one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd dig in on the customer side, make sure the big accounts ask for me by name, so I'm hard to cut. I'd stop spending on the extras for the wedding, the band and the second venue. And I'd ask my uncle Samuel, who's an electrician with his own firm, what it would take to start an apprenticeship, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Annoyed, more than anything, that this is being done to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've avoided the new systems. Would you learn them now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the minimum they make me do. I know that's stubborn, and Grace tells me so. But I don't want to be the one who teaches the machine how to replace my own lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we keep the date but go smaller. Her mother wants the big do, and I'd have to be the one to say it. A wedding is a promise, not a party, so it'll be fine.

say: Our customers **like a person** and would go to a competitor.
Big tech is **selling bosses a dream** to cut wages.
Work gives people **dignity**, and a machine can't replace that.
think: Head office would **do it anyway**, and I'm on the wrong side.
I've **avoided the new systems**, so I'd struggle to keep a manager job.
do: Make the **big accounts** ask for me by name.
Cut the **wedding extras**: the band and the second venue.
Ask **uncle Samuel** about an electrician apprenticeship.
feel: **Worried**, and more **annoyed** that this is being done to us.
S1.quote: Booking, checking and answering customers is my order desk at the brick works, near enough word for word.
fieldNote: His job **matches the card** almost word for word, and he knows it.
He'd **refuse to train** the system that replaces his own team.
A **family trade** is his fallback, not learning AI.

steps.text: Get the big building accounts asking for me by name
Drop the band and second venue from the wedding plans
Ask uncle Samuel about starting an electrician apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then I'm finished at Calder, simple as that. If a computer can do almost any thinking work, it can take orders and book lorries, and it won't need me to manage it. The robots for the factory floor come later, but I don't work on the factory floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that companies and government let this happen with no warning. I'd sign whatever petition was going round to slow it down. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, because the government won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be out within a year. I'd have savings and a flat, so I wouldn't go hungry, but I'd be a 29-year-old office manager with nothing a machine can't do, and that scares me more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd call uncle Samuel and ask to start as his apprentice electrician, even on apprentice pay. I'd push the wedding back a year, which would break Grace's heart, but I'm not starting a marriage with no job. And I'd stop putting money into anything but the savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry. I'd be up at night going over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrician, given robots come about three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three years is three years, and wiring someone's old house isn't like stacking boxes. I reckon a robot that can find a fault in a 1950s kitchen will take longer than people think. And it's a trade, it's something you can hand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd postpone the wedding. What would Grace say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm being proud, and that we could manage on her teaching salary. She'd be right about the money. But I was raised that the man brings in a wage, and I'd want that sorted before we marry.

say: It's a **disgrace** that firms and government gave **no warning**.
I'd **sign any petition** to slow it down.
At church I'd say we must **look after each other**.
think: I'd be **out within a year** at Calder.
Having nothing a machine can't do **scares me more** than money.
do: Start as uncle Samuel's **apprentice electrician** in the first month.
feel: **Frightened and angry**, and up at night going over it.
S2.quote: I'd be a 29-year-old office manager with nothing a machine can't do, and that scares me more than the money.
fieldNote: He sees **no hands-on buffer** in his desk job, so the date hits at once.
His fallback is a **family trade**, which he trusts more than the robot timeline.
**Pride about providing** drives the wedding delay more than money does.

steps.text: Start as uncle Samuel's apprentice electrician in the first month
Push the wedding with Grace back a year
Put all spare money into the savings account
Sign petitions calling for the AI rollout to slow down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better, but it's still the end of my kind of job. I'd be 32, married, maybe with a baby on the way. At least I'd have time to do it properly instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so the government should fund apprenticeships, real ones, not online courses. At work I'd tell the younger lads on the desk to learn a trade while they can. I'd still say the tech firms are getting rich off everyone else's jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know Calder would cut the desk by 2031 and I'd be gone with it. I'm still not going to become an AI person, that's not me. But five years is enough to finish an electrical apprenticeship and be qualified before the robots, which come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Calder for two more years while doing evening classes in electrical installation. Then I'd move over to uncle Samuel's firm full time around 2029, with Grace's blessing. We'd keep the wedding date but put off a bigger house until I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see a road. That makes a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go from a manager's salary to a trainee's pay. How does that sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well, if I'm honest. It's maybe half what I earn now for the first couple of years. But I've got savings for exactly that reason, and my dad always said a trade is worth more than a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots arrive around 2034, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be 35 with a trade and maybe running jobs for Samuel. I don't know what robots will manage by then, nobody does. But I'd rather face the robots with an electrician's toolbag than with a sales desk that's already gone.

Join **uncle Samuel's firm** full time around 2029.

S3.quote: I'd rather face the robots with an electrician's toolbag than with a sales desk that's already gone.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **plan the switch** to a trade instead of panicking.
He accepts a **half-pay training** period, cushioned by savings and his father's advice.
He still **rejects learning AI**; his whole answer is a hands-on trade.

steps.text: Take evening classes in electrical installation while still at Calder
Join uncle Samuel's electrical firm full time around 2029
Put off buying a bigger house until qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Plenty can happen in ten years, and I've seen a lot of predictions come to nothing. I'd be 37, probably with two kids, and I'd want to have something solid by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see. Ten years out, half of these forecasts will be wrong. At work I'd probably say we've got plenty of time and there's no point losing sleep yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know it'd come for the desk eventually. The danger for me is that I'd leave it too late, because I'm not one for change. I'd probably wait until about 2030 and then wish I'd started sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd keep my head down at Calder and go for the regional manager job. I'd keep saving and pay off a chunk of the flat so the mortgage is small when the kids come. Around 2030 I'd start the electrician course with uncle Samuel, if things were clearly heading that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too bad day to day, but there's a worry sitting in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until about 2030. What would tell you it's time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Calder started cutting people on the order desk, that'd be my signal. Or if Mr Haldane at the Birchfield yard started placing orders through a computer instead of calling me. That would tell me the customers had moved on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd still try for kids after the wedding, that's not up for debate for us. Children are a blessing, not something you schedule around a computer.

say: **Let's see**; half these forecasts will be wrong in ten years.
We've got **plenty of time**, so no point losing sleep yet.
think: AI would **come for the desk** eventually.
My danger is **leaving it too late**, because I'm not one for change.
do: Go for the **regional manager** job and keep my head down.
**Pay off part** of the flat before the kids come.
Start the **electrician course** around 2030 if things clearly shift.
feel: Fine day to day, with a **worry** in the back of my mind.
S4.quote: Children are a blessing, not something you schedule around a computer.
fieldNote: The long window lets his **resistance to change** take over; he'd wait for clear signals.
His **signal** would be a loyal customer ordering by computer instead of phoning him.
**Children** after the wedding are fixed, whatever AI does.

steps.text: Go for the regional sales manager job at Calder
Pay off a chunk of the flat mortgage before children come
Wait for order desk cuts before starting the electrician course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. No time to learn a trade, no time to save more, and a wedding on top of it. What would help is the government paying for proper apprenticeships for people like me who want to switch to real work. Not handouts, I don't want a cheque for sitting at home, I want a way to earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For me, a lot of this comes down to whether work still means something. If machines do all the work, I worry what men my age do with themselves. That's not something a computer can answer.

headlineQuote: If machines do all the work, I worry what men my age do with themselves.
portrait: Emeka is an **order desk manager**, aged 27, at Calder Building Products, engaged to Grace.
He has **never used AI**, distrusts it, and values customers, church and family.
He is **uneasy** in AI Plateau, with orders already down ten percent.
Steady Disruption and **fast AGI** push him towards an electrician apprenticeship with his uncle.
With **ten years**, he admits he'd likely wait too long to act.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to learn a trade and a **wedding** coming.
whatWouldHelp: **Government-funded apprenticeships** for people switching into trades.
**A way to earn**, not handouts for sitting at home.
